summary.text: Hiroshima is the capital of Hiroshima Prefecture in Japan, a city founded in 1589 as a castle town on the Ōta River delta.
On 6 August 1945 the United States Army Air Forces dropped the atomic bomb "Little Boy" on it, making it the first military target of a nuclear weapon in history.
Most of the city was destroyed, and by the end of the year between 90,000 and 166,000 people had died from the blast and its effects.

facts.label: A-Bomb Dome
facts.value: The only structure left standing, kept as a preserved ruin

paragraphs.heading: A castle town on a delta
paragraphs.text: Hiroshima is a city in Japan and the capital of Hiroshima Prefecture. Its name means "wide island" in Japanese. Before the city existed, the spot was a small fishing village on the shore of Hiroshima Bay. In 1589 the powerful warlord Mōri Terumoto founded a castle town on the delta of the Ōta River, at the edge of the Seto Inland Sea. Hiroshima Castle went up fast, and Mōri moved into it in 1593.

paragraphs.heading: Changing hands
paragraphs.text: Terumoto backed the side that lost the Battle of Sekigahara. The winner, Tokugawa Ieyasu, stripped him of most of his lands, Hiroshima among them. From 1619 the Asano clan governed the town. Their rule lasted until 1871, when the Han was abolished and Hiroshima became the capital of its prefecture.

paragraphs.heading: The morning of 6 August 1945
paragraphs.text: Bombing raids caused widespread destruction in Tokyo and other cities of Japan, but no such raids hit Hiroshima. People still saw the danger, and children aged 11 to 14 were set to work pulling down houses to make firebreaks. At 8:15 a.m. on Monday, 6 August 1945, a B-29 bomber named the Enola Gay, piloted by Paul Tibbets, dropped the atomic bomb "Little Boy" on the city. No city had ever before been the military target of a nuclear weapon. The blast directly killed at least 70,000 people, thousands of Korean slave labourers among them.

paragraphs.heading: The toll
paragraphs.text: Most of Hiroshima was wiped out. By the end of that year, somewhere between 90,000 and 166,000 people had died from the blast and what followed it.

paragraphs.heading: The dome that stayed
paragraphs.text: In 1915 an exhibition hall was built as a centre for trade and for showing new products, and the building was renamed twice afterwards. Today it is called the A-Bomb Dome. It is kept as a preserved ruin and is part of the Hiroshima Peace Memorial, which has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996 and stands as a memorial to the bombing.

paragraphs.heading: Rebuilt
paragraphs.text: Hiroshima was rebuilt after the war. No city in the Chūgoku region, in the west of Honshu, is now larger. It had an estimated 1,170,194 people living there as of 1 August 2026.
